title: Emor: the poor at the feast (Leviticus 23:22)
hookLine: in the middle of the festivals, a reminder to leave gleanings for the poor

lines: THE GOOD DISHES, TOO MUCH FOOD.
cards: A holiday table. The good dishes, the long tablecloth, too much food, cousins arguing about seating. The best kind of chaos.
And somewhere in the same city, at the same hour, someone is eating alone, or not eating much at all. Leviticus 23 has been walking through the festivals in order: Passover, the omer, Shavuot.
Next should come the seventh month, the new year. But right there, in between, the Torah stops the calendar for one verse that isn't about a festival at all.

teach.b: Right after Shavuot, the harvest feast, the verse says: when you reap your field, don't reap its corner fully, or gather the gleanings.

In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, "thou shalt leave them for the poor, and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God." You heard almost the same words in Kedoshim, a week ago. So why say it again, here?
Rashi cites a rabbi named Avdimi, who asks exactly that: why put the gifts for the poor in the middle of the festivals?

teach.h: RASHI: AS IF YOU BUILT THE TEMPLE.
teach.b: To teach that whoever leaves the gleanings and the corner properly is considered as if they had built the Temple and brought offerings in it. Feeding the poor sits among the holiest days, and counts like an offering.
Maimonides rules that when you eat and drink on a festival, you must also feed the stranger, the orphan, the widow, and others in need.
And he's blunt: someone who locks their doors and feasts only with their own family isn't celebrating a commandment.

teach.h: NOT THE JOY OF THE STOMACH.
teach.b: That, he says, is the joy of their stomach.

teach.h: LET ALL WHO ARE HUNGRY COME.
teach.b: Early in the Passover seder, well before the meal, the table hears the words: let all who are hungry come and eat. On Purim, gifts to the poor are part of the day itself.
A Jewish feast is supposed to have an open edge, like a field with its corners left uncut.

how: Jewish festivals include giving: the Passover seder's telling opens with an invitation to the hungry, Purim includes matanot la'evyonim, gifts to the poor, and some families give tzedakah before Shabbat and holidays.

o: the festival calendar, from spring to fall
say: the portion of priests and festivals
gleanings, the stalks left for the poor

games.q: what's inside the verse — tap the pairs.
p: between Shavuot and the seventh month
as if you built the Temple
let all who are hungry come

s: the gleanings verse in Leviticus 23 appears nowhere else
nearly the same law is in Leviticus 19, in Kedoshim.
Rashi says leaving gleanings is like building the Temple
citing Rabbi Avdimi, on why the verse sits among the festivals.
Maimonides says feasting only with family fulfills the festival
without feeding those in need, he calls it the joy of the stomach.

games.q: it's the festival. your table is full, your doors are locked, your family is happy. what does Maimonides say?
o: this is the joy of the festival.
this is the joy of your stomach.
this is fine if you gave last month.
games.why: without feeding the stranger, the orphan and the widow, he calls it the joy of the stomach, not of a commandment.

practice: Picture the next celebration on your calendar, a holiday, a birthday, a dinner out, and an empty chair at the table.

Who could that chair be for: a neighbor alone for the holiday, a student far from home, a food bank, a gift in someone's name? Let one way of giving become part of the celebration itself, not something after it.

wordCard.voice: Emor. The portion that pauses its calendar of feasts to remind the reapers to leave something for the poor and the stranger.

orig.note: Hebrew: gleanings, the stalks that fall in the harvest and are left for the poor.

carryVoice: Your line: remember them at the feast. The good dishes can stretch to one more plate. Day four hundred eighteen, done.

sources.q: thou shalt leave them for the poor, and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God.
